title: Why the Sky Is Blue
subtitle: One sunbeam explains blue noons and red sunsets
objectives: Explain why white sunlight is a mix of colours with different wavelengths
Describe what scattering is, and why short waves scatter far more than long ones
Use that one rule to explain both the blue sky and red sunsets
Say why the sky looks blue rather than violet

lines: The air around you is completely see-through.
Yet look up on a clear day, and the whole sky glows blue.
At sunset, that very same sky turns orange and red.
One simple rule explains both, and it all happens inside a single sunbeam.
Start with sunlight itself, which looks white.
Shine it through a prism, and it fans out into a rainbow, from red to violet.
So white light is really every colour, travelling together.
Each colour is a wave, and the only difference between colours is the wave's length.

lines.text: Red waves are long, about 700 nanometres. Blue waves are shorter, about 450.
lines.say: Red waves are long, about seven hundred nanometres. Blue waves are shorter, about four hundred and fifty.

lines: A nanometre is a billionth of a metre, so these waves are very, very small.
Now, the air: mostly nitrogen and oxygen molecules, with lots of empty space between them.
Each molecule is more than a thousand times smaller than a wave of light.
Most sunlight sails straight past them, which is why air looks clear up close.
But now and then, a wave meets a molecule and gets sent off in a random new direction.
That is called scattering.
Here's the key: short waves get scattered far more than long ones.
A passing light wave shakes the electrons inside a molecule, and they send out light of their own, in every direction.
Shorter waves shake them faster, and faster shaking sends out much more light.
Physicists call this Rayleigh scattering: halve the wavelength, and the scattering goes up sixteen times.
So blue light ends up scattered about six times more than red.
Now stand on the ground and look at a patch of sky, away from the sun.
Any light reaching you from there was scattered toward your eyes on its way through the air.
And scattered light is mostly blue, so the whole sky glows blue.
On the Moon, with no air to scatter anything, the sky is black, even at noon.
At sunset, sunlight reaches you at a low angle, through far more air.
Along that long path, most of the blue is scattered away before it ever reaches you.
What's left in the beam is the long-wave light: orange and red.
Same rule, opposite side: the scattered light is blue, and the light that gets through is red.
One last puzzle: violet waves are even shorter than blue, so why isn't the sky violet?
First, sunlight contains less violet than blue to begin with, and some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere.
Second, our eyes are much less sensitive to violet than to blue.
Mix it all together, and our eyes read the sky as a soft, pale blue.
So: sunlight is a mix of colours, each a wave of a different length.
Air molecules scatter short blue waves far more than long red ones.
Look away from the sun and you see scattered blue; look through lots of air at sunset and you see the red that's left.
